# Kiṁpakkajātaka (Ja 85)

**ID:** Ja 85
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kiṁpakkajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Unknown Fruit
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja85
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kiṁpakkajātaka* (Ja 85) is a short narrative belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Set at Jetavana, the introductory story relates that the Buddha addressed a monk who was troubled by lustful longing (*ukkanṭhita*) after seeing an elaborately adorned woman during his almsround in Sāvatthī [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Opening with the verse incipit *Āyatiṁ dosaṁ nāññāya*, the Buddha relates a past life in which he was a caravan leader (*satthavāho*) [Fausböll 1877]. In that past existence, members of his caravan ignored his warnings and consumed the sweet, fragrant fruit of the *kimpakka* tree—mistaking its appearance, boughs, and taste for those of a mango tree—which resulted in their severe poisoning and death [Deleanu 2006; Lamotte; Fausböll 1877].

In broader Buddhist literature, the *kimpāka* fruit serves as a prominent metaphor illustrating the deceptive allure and fatal consequences of sensual pleasures [Deleanu 2006]. The text was edited by V. Fausböll in the Pali Text Society edition of the Jātaka commentary (Vol. I, pp. 367–369) [Fausböll 1877; Deleanu 2006]. An early English rendering was produced by Robert Chalmers, who translated *kimpakka* literally as the "what-fruit" [Deleanu 2006], and SuttaCentral registers four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].

Neither SuttaCentral nor the automated text-reuse matches in DharmaNexus identify any canonical cross-language parallels or Pali-internal text reuse for this discourse [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. However, Étienne Lamotte cites the Jātaka in comparative annotation to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra* when discussing analogous Indian folktales of poisonous or wondrous fruits [Lamotte].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja85 — Supplied title, introductory blurb, and translation counts.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel analysis database — Confirmed absence of automated Pali-internal reuse and cross-language matches.
- [Deleanu 2006] Florin Deleanu, The Chapter on the Mundane Path (Laukikamārga) in the Śrāvakabhūmi, Vol. 2 (2006) — Discussed the kimpāka fruit metaphor, Chalmers's English translation, and textual descriptions of the fruit.
- [Fausböll 1877] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 1 (1877) — Provided the Pali edition, verse incipit, setting at Jetavana, and the Bodhisatta's role as caravan leader.
- [Lamotte] Étienne Lamotte, Le Traité de la Grande Vertu de Sagesse de Nāgārjuna (Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra), Vol. 2 — Noted the story of the caravan eating kimpaka fruit mistaken for mangoes in comparison with the Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra.
